Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5: seventy persons of Jacob's house came to Egypt.
Numbers 1:46 counts 603,550 fighting men at Sinai.

Others agree it was fulfilled in that way but note that the promise also points further. Paul and Hebrews link Abraham's countless seed to all nations who believe (Romans 4:16-18; Hebrews 11:12). They see this as a number-image, not a sign that the sky means Israel.
What did Joseph's dream of the sun, moon and eleven stars mean?
Jacob knew at once: the sun and moon were himself and Joseph's mother, and the eleven stars were Joseph's brothers. The heavenly lights stood for the family of Israel.

Joseph dreamed that the sun, the moon and eleven stars bowed to him (Genesis 37:9). Jacob did not need an interpreter. He asked, "Shall I and your mother and your brothers bow down to you?" (37:10). The covenantal reading notes this carefully. In the family of promise, the lights of heaven were a picture of the covenant household. The father was the sun, the mother the moon, and the sons the stars. Years later the dream came true when the brothers bowed in Egypt (Genesis 42:6). Revelation 12:1 uses the same picture: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and twelve stars on her head, standing for Israel as God's people.
Genesis 42:6: Joseph's brothers bowed with their faces to the ground before him in Egypt.
Revelation 12:1-5: the woman with sun, moon and twelve stars gives birth to the male child who rules the nations.

All readers accept that the dream used heavenly lights as symbols. Traditional readers say the dream was a symbolic vision, so it shows that sky images can stand for people in dreams and visions. They do not see it as proof that "heaven and earth" means Israel in plain statements.
Do the physical heavens "utter speech" (Psalms 19:1-4)?
Not with words. The psalm itself says there is no speech or language. The covenantal reading says the "heavens" that pour out words are also a picture of God's people spreading his message.

Psalms 19:1-2 says the heavens tell God's glory, and day after day they pour out speech. Verse 3 adds that there is no speech or words, and no voice is heard. Verse 4 says their line goes out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world. The writer speaks of "their words" and "in them". The covenantal reading asks: can sky and stars really speak? It answers that the psalm uses the heavens as a picture. The second half of the psalm (19:7-11) praises God's law. So the psalm joins creation and covenant. On this reading, the heavens that speak point to a people who carry God's word. Paul confirms this use in Romans 10:18.
Psalms 19:3 in Hebrew can be read "there is no speech... their voice is not heard": silent speech.
Psalms 19:7-11 turns from the sun to the law of the Lord, which revives the soul.

Most readers say Psalm 19 describes the silent witness of the real sky, which "speaks" by showing God's power to everyone (Romans 1:20). They see the psalm as moving from God's word in creation (verses 1-6) to his word in Scripture (verses 7-14), both real and both glorious.
Who declares God's glory: the stars, or God's people?

Both readings agree creation shows his glory. The covenantal reading stresses that Paul quotes Psalms 19:4 for preachers of the gospel, so God's people are the "heavens" whose voice goes to all the earth.

In Romans 10:14-18 Paul asks how people will hear without a preacher. Then he asks, "Have they not heard?" and quotes Psalms 19:4: their voice went out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. Paul applies the words of the "heavens" to the messengers of Christ. On the covenantal reading, this is the key. The New Testament itself reads Psalm 19 about a people who declare God's glory. Psalms 96:3 also tells God's people to declare his glory among the nations. Isaiah 43:21 says God formed a people to declare his praise. So the heavens declare God's glory most clearly when his people speak.
Romans 10:18 quotes Psalms 19:4 word for word from the Greek Old Testament, applied to gospel preachers.
Colossians 1:23: the gospel had been preached "to every creature under heaven" by about AD 60.

Many commentators say Paul borrows the psalm's words as an analogy: as the sky's witness is everywhere, so the gospel has gone everywhere. They do not think Paul is saying the heavens in Psalm 19 meant preachers. Paul elsewhere says creation itself shows God (Romans 1:20).
Is the sun coming out like a bridegroom (Psalms 19:4-6) a picture of Christ?
The covenantal reading sees a prophetic hint of Christ the bridegroom and the "sun of righteousness". Others see a poetic picture of the real sun's daily course.

Psalms 19:4-5 says God set a tent for the sun, which comes out like a bridegroom from his room and runs its course like a strong man. Nothing is hidden from its heat. The covenantal reading notes the bridegroom image. Jesus calls himself the bridegroom (Matthew 9:15). Malachi 4:2 speaks of the sun of righteousness rising with healing. Zechariah, John the Baptist's father, spoke of the "dayspring from on high" visiting us (Luke 1:78). On this reading, Psalm 19 uses the sun to speak of the coming Messiah who brings light to all. The "tent" set for the sun matches God's tabernacle among his people. The psalm is creation language used for covenant purposes.
Malachi 4:2: "the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings" (KJV).
Matthew 17:2: at the transfiguration Jesus' face shone like the sun.

Most scholars see verses 4-6 as praise for the actual sun, using a bridegroom and a runner to show its joy and strength. Some Christian writers since the Church Fathers saw Christ in it by analogy, but not as the psalm's main sense.
Does the covenantal reading deny that the physical heavens show God's glory?
No. Its supporters say the physical world is glorious and shows God's power. They only argue that many "heaven and earth" texts use creation as a picture of a greater covenant glory.

The covenantal reading does not deny creation. Its writers say they praise God for the stars, the sea and the land. Romans 1:20 says God's power and nature are clearly seen in what he made. Psalms 8:3 marvels at the moon and stars. Job 38-41 shows God pointing Job to the real sky, sea and animals. The covenantal reading claims something extra. In many passages, the focus is not the physical world but what it pictures: God's relationship with his people. On this reading, creation's glory points to a greater glory, the new creation in Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). The God who said "Let light shine" has shone in our hearts.
2 Corinthians 4:6: Paul links "light shall shine out of darkness" (Genesis 1:3) with the light of the gospel in the heart.
Psalms 8:3-4: "When I consider your heavens... what is man?"

Critics worry that the reading drifts toward treating the material world as unimportant. They point out that God called creation "very good" (Genesis 1:31), raised Jesus bodily (Luke 24:39), and promises that creation itself will be set free (Romans 8:21). They think the future of matter matters too.
Do fish and whales praise the Lord (Psalms 69:34)?
The covenantal reading says no in a literal sense. Psalms 69:34-35 calls heaven, earth and seas to praise "for God will save Zion". It is God's saved people who praise him.

Psalms 69:30 begins with one person: "I will praise the name of God with a song." Verse 34 then says, "Let heaven and earth praise him, the seas and everything that moves in them." Verse 35 gives the reason: "For God will save Zion and build the cities of Judah." On the covenantal reading, it would be odd for sea creatures to praise God for saving Zion. Those who praise are those who love God and belong to him. Verse 36 says the children of his servants will inherit the land. So heaven, earth and sea in this psalm picture the people of God, near and far, who rejoice in his salvation.
Psalms 69:32: "The humble shall see this and be glad"; the praise comes from God's people.
Isaiah 60:5 calls the nations "the abundance of the sea" coming to Zion.

Most readers say creatures "praise" God by being what he made them to be, as Psalm 148 calls sea monsters, hail and trees to praise him. Revelation 5:13 has every creature in sea and earth praising the Lamb. They see this as real creation joining in, not only a picture of people.
What is God's glory "above the heavens" in Psalms 113:4-6?
God is higher than all nations and all the heavens, yet he bends down to look at heaven and earth. The covenantal reading recalls the pillar of cloud and fire over Israel.

Psalms 113:4 says the Lord is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens. Verses 5-6 say he lives on high, yet humbles himself to see what is in heaven and on earth. Verses 7-9 tell of him lifting the poor from the dust and giving the childless woman a home. On the covenantal reading, the psalm sets "heaven and earth" in the setting of God's care for his people. It also recalls the exodus, when God's glory went above Israel in the cloud by day and the fire by night (Exodus 13:21). The God above all comes down to save the lowly. That is covenant, not astronomy.
Exodus 40:34-38: the cloud of glory covered and filled the tabernacle.
Psalms 113:7-8: God lifts the poor from the dust and seats them with princes.

Most readers see the psalm as praising God as higher than the whole universe and yet close to the humble. They agree it stresses covenant mercy, but read "heaven and earth" in verse 6 as the whole created order under his eye.
How are heaven and earth God's "servants" (Psalms 119:89-91)?

The psalm says God's word is fixed in heaven, he established the earth, and "all things are your servants". The covenantal reading sees covenant faithfulness to his people. The natural sense is creation obeying God's laws.

Psalms 119:89 says God's word is settled in heaven forever. Verse 90 says his faithfulness lasts through all generations, and he established the earth so it stands. Verse 91 says they continue to this day by his ordinances, for all are his servants. The covenantal reading notes that "faithfulness" and "generations" are covenant words. Heaven and earth serve God as his people serve him. It also links the "ordinances" to the fixed order God swore by in Jeremiah 31:35-36. A careful reader will note that this same reasoning shows the physical earth "abides". So the psalm supports the view that the material world continues, while God's word governs both creation and covenant.
Jeremiah 33:25 calls the order of day and night God's "covenant" with heaven and earth.
Psalms 104:4 calls wind and fire God's servants.
Most commentators read this as creation obeying God's set laws, which shows that his word can be trusted. They say "servants" means creation does his will, as in Psalms 104:4 and 148:8.
Who declares God's righteousness (Psalms 50:4-6; 97:6; 22:31)?
The heavens, in Psalm 50, and also a people yet to be born, in Psalm 22. The covenantal reading says Psalm 50 calls heaven and earth to judge "his people", and the declaring is done by God's people.

Psalms 50:4 says God calls to the heavens above and to the earth "that he may judge his people". Verse 5 says, "Gather my saints to me, those who made a covenant with me by sacrifice." Verse 6: "The heavens declare his righteousness." Psalms 97:6 says the heavens declare his righteousness and all peoples see his glory. Psalms 22:31 says they will come and declare his righteousness to a people yet to be born. On the covenantal reading, the setting is a covenant trial. God gathers his covenant people. Those who declare his righteousness are people: the saints and the generations who tell what God has done.
Psalms 50:5: the gathering is of those "who made a covenant with me by sacrifice".
Psalms 22:30-31: a seed will serve him; they will tell the next generation what he has done.

Others see heaven and earth in Psalm 50 as witnesses in a court scene, as in Deuteronomy 32:1, while God judges his people. They agree that the covenant is central but say the heavens are called as witnesses, not as the people being judged.
What does it mean that the wicked "set their mouth against the heavens" (Psalms 73:9)?
The arrogant speak against God and his rule, and their words spread over the land. The covenantal reading sees attacks on God and his covenant people, not on the sky.

Psalms 73:8-9 describes proud people who mock and speak with malice. They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongues strut through the earth. Nobody speaks against the sky for its own sake. "Heavens" here stands for God and his throne, and "earth" for people and life in the land. On the covenantal reading, the line shows how "heaven and earth" can describe the realm of God and his people. The wicked speak against God above and trouble people below. Verse 10 says "his people" turn to them. The psalm resolves when Asaph goes into "the sanctuary of God" (73:17), the place where heaven and earth meet.
Psalms 73:17: Asaph understood their end only when he went into God's sanctuary.
Revelation 13:6: the beast opens its mouth to blaspheme God, his tabernacle, and those who dwell in heaven.

Most readers agree "heavens" here means God and his authority, by a common figure of speech (Luke 15:18). They see it as poetry for pride that reaches up to God and out to all people, not as evidence about the meaning of "heaven and earth" elsewhere.
Why should "the heavens rejoice and the earth be glad" (Psalms 96:11; 1 Chronicles 16:31)?
Because "the Lord reigns" and is coming to judge the peoples. The covenantal reading says the joy belongs to the nations who hear of God's rule, the people pictured as heaven, earth and sea.

Psalms 96:10 says to tell the nations that the Lord reigns. The world is established, and he will judge the peoples fairly. Verse 11 says let the heavens rejoice and the earth be glad; let the sea roar. Verse 13 says he comes to judge the earth. David first sang this when he brought the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:23-33). On the covenantal reading, the joy is the joy of peoples who learn of God's rule. The call to "say among the nations" shows that people are the focus. The rejoicing heavens and earth picture God's people and the nations brought into his worship.
1 Chronicles 16:31: "Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice; let men say among the nations, The Lord reigns."
David brought the ark to Jerusalem about 1000 BC; this song was sung that day.

Most readers see the whole creation joining in praise, as rivers clap and hills sing in Psalms 98:8. They link this to Romans 8:21, where creation waits for freedom. They see the joy as both human and cosmic.
What heavens and earth "perish" and are changed like a garment (Psalms 102:25-27; Hebrews 1:10-12)?

The psalm contrasts God, who stays the same, with heavens and earth that wear out. Hebrews applies it to the Son. The covenantal reading links the "old garment" to the old covenant that was growing old.

Psalms 102:25-26 says God laid the earth's foundation and made the heavens, but they will perish. They will wear out like clothing. Like a robe he will change them. Hebrews 1:10-12 quotes this about the Son. A few chapters later Hebrews uses the same idea: the first covenant is "growing old" and near to vanishing (Hebrews 8:13). On the covenantal reading, the writer of Hebrews tells us which heavens and earth were wearing out. It was the old covenant order. Psalms 102:28 then promises that the children of God's servants will continue. A new people stands when the old order is folded up.
Hebrews 1:11 and 8:13 use the same idea of "growing old" (the Greek verb palaioo).
Jesus spoke of not putting new cloth on an old garment (Matthew 9:16), a picture of the new not patching the old.

Most readers see the psalm and Hebrews 1 as speaking of the real created universe, which is temporary next to the eternal Son. They link it to Hebrews 12:27 and 2 Peter 3:10 and expect the cosmos to be changed or renewed at Christ's return.
What do Jeremiah 31:35-36 and 33:20-21 mean when they tie God's covenant to the sun, moon and stars?

God says his covenant will stand as surely as day and night. If the fixed order of the sky could fail, his promise could fail. The fulfilled reading uses this to say the physical heavens do not pass away.

In Jeremiah 31:31-34 God promises a new covenant. In 31:35-36 he says: if the fixed order of sun, moon and stars departs, then Israel's seed will stop being a nation before him. In 33:20-21 he says: if you can break my covenant with day and night, then you can break my covenant with David. Psalms 89:36-37 says David's throne will last like the sun and the moon, the faithful witness in the sky. On the fulfilled reading, two points follow. First, the new covenant and David's throne, now held by Christ, are as lasting as the sky. Second, the physical sky is not about to vanish. So the heaven and earth that passed in Jesus' generation must be the old covenant order.
Luke 1:32-33: the angel says God will give Jesus the throne of David and his kingdom will have no end.
Jeremiah 33:25-26 repeats the oath: if I have not set the fixed laws of heaven and earth, then I will reject David's seed.

Dispensationalists read "Israel will not cease to be a nation" as a promise to ethnic Israel, still in force. Covenant theologians apply it to the Israel of God in Christ (Galatians 6:16). Many note that the oath is about God's faithfulness, not a claim that the cosmos never changes.
Do the physical heavens and earth come under God's judgment?
The covenantal reading says sky and soil do not sin, so they are not judged. When prophets show heavens shaken and earth burned, they speak of peoples and rulers judged by God.

In the prophets, heaven and earth are shaken, darkened, rolled up and burned. Who is judged? Sin belongs to people. Isaiah 13:11 says, right in the middle of the darkened sky, "I will punish the world for its evil and the wicked for their sin." Isaiah 24:5 says the earth is defiled because its people broke the everlasting covenant. On the covenantal reading, the cosmic pictures describe God's judgment on nations and their leaders. The sun and moon are kings and powers. The earth is the people in the land. God does not hold rocks guilty. He judges people, and the prophets use the language of a collapsing world to show how total that judgment is.
Isaiah 13:10-11 puts "stars will not give light" and "I will punish the world for its evil" side by side.
Genesis 3:17: the ground was cursed "because of you" — the curse came on creation because of human sin.

Others agree that people, not matter, are guilty. But they say creation suffers because of human sin (Genesis 3:17; Romans 8:20). So creation can be shaken as part of God's judgment on people, and later set free. Its judgment is a side effect, not a punishment for its own sin.
Do the physical heavens and earth need to be redeemed?
The covenantal reading says redemption is for people, not for stars. Others point to Romans 8:19-22, where creation itself waits to be set free from decay.

Redemption in Scripture means buying back a person from slavery or guilt (Exodus 6:6; Ephesians 1:7). Stars and rocks have not sinned, so they do not need forgiveness. On the covenantal reading, this is why texts about heaven and earth being judged and made new are about people. The Bible's main story is God and the redemption of his people. That fits a covenant new creation better than a remade cosmos. Some covenantal readers take Romans 8:19-22 as speaking of the "creation" of humanity, Jew and Gentile, groaning for the revealing of God's sons. They also note that Paul says "if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation" (2 Corinthians 5:17).
Ephesians 1:7: in Christ we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins.
Colossians 1:23: Paul says the gospel was preached "to every creature (ktisis) under heaven" — the same word as "creation" in Romans 8, used for people.

Most interpreters read Romans 8:19-22 as the non-human creation, which was subjected to futility and will share the freedom of God's children. They link this with the bodily resurrection and with "restoration of all things" (Acts 3:21; Colossians 1:20). For them, God redeems people and renews their world.
What did Isaiah mean by a darkened sun and a shaken earth in his oracle on Babylon (Isaiah 13:10-13)?
He described the fall of Babylon to the Medes in 539 BC. The cosmic words picture the collapse of a world empire, not the end of the universe.

Isaiah 13:1 names the subject: "The burden of Babylon." Verse 10 says the stars, sun and moon will not give their light. Verse 13 says God will shake the heavens and move the earth from its place. Verse 17 names the attackers: the Medes. Verse 19 says Babylon will become like Sodom. On the fulfilled reading, this shows how prophets speak. A real empire fell in history, but the prophet used the language of a dying sky. Note: one argument says the pronoun "her" ("her light", "her place") proves that a people is meant. That is weak. "Her" comes from English and Hebrew grammar. The stronger point is the context, which names Babylon and the Medes.
Babylon fell to Cyrus' Medo-Persian army in October 539 BC (Nabonidus Chronicle; Daniel 5:30-31).
Isaiah 13:17 names the Medes as the attackers, about 150 years before they came.

Almost all scholars agree Isaiah 13 is about Babylon's fall and uses figurative cosmic language. Some futurists see a double meaning, with a future end-time Babylon (Revelation 18). Others say Isaiah 13:9-13 widens to the final day of the Lord over the whole world.
Did the sky really roll up like a scroll over Edom (Isaiah 34:4), and did the stars go dark over Egypt (Ezekiel 32:7-8)?
No. These were judgments on real nations, Edom and Egypt. The prophets used the language of a collapsing sky for the fall of their power.

Isaiah 34:4 says the host of heaven will dissolve, the sky will roll up like a scroll, and the stars will fall like leaves. Verse 5 explains: God's sword will come down on Edom, the people he has judged. Ezekiel 32:2 addresses Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Verses 7-8 say that when God puts him out, he will cover the heavens, darken the stars and the sun, and bring darkness on his land. On the fulfilled reading, the sky did not literally roll up. Edom and Egypt fell. These are the same words Jesus uses in Matthew 24:29 and John uses in Revelation 6:13-14. They describe the end of a nation's order.
Edom was overrun by Arab tribes and the Nabataeans by the 4th century BC (Malachi 1:3-4 already sees it desolate).
Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt's power at Carchemish in 605 BC and invaded Egypt about 568 BC.

Scholars widely agree that these texts are figurative for historical judgments. Futurists say Revelation 6:13-14 uses the same words for a final, worldwide judgment, so the pattern points to an ultimate fulfilment. Many amillennialists see both a near and an ultimate sense.
Who is addressed in "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth" (Isaiah 1:2)?
The message is about Judah and Jerusalem (1:1). The covenantal reading says Isaiah, like Moses, calls the covenant people "heaven and earth". Others say he calls creation as a witness.

Isaiah 1:1 says the vision concerns Judah and Jerusalem. Verse 2 begins, "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I raised children, and they rebelled against me." Verse 10 then calls the leaders "rulers of Sodom" and the people "people of Gomorrah". On the covenantal reading, Isaiah copies Moses (Deuteronomy 32:1). He speaks to a covenant nation in the language of heaven and earth. The whole book then moves from the judgment of this old "heaven and earth" to the promise of new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22). The book opens and closes with heaven and earth, and both are about God's people.
Isaiah opens with heaven and earth (1:2) and closes with new heavens and new earth (66:22).
Isaiah 1:10 calls Jerusalem's rulers "rulers of Sodom", a picture-name for a covenant people.

Most scholars see a covenant lawsuit: God calls heaven and earth as witnesses, as Moses did, and then charges Israel. The witnesses and the accused are different. This keeps the covenant setting but reads heaven and earth as creation.
Why are the heavens, earth, mountains and forests told to sing when God redeems Jacob (Isaiah 44:23; 49:13)?
Because God has redeemed and comforted his people. The covenantal reading says the singers are people pictured as heavens, earth, mountains and trees.

Isaiah 44:23 says: sing, O heavens; shout, depths of the earth; break into song, mountains, forest and every tree, "for the Lord has redeemed Jacob". Isaiah 49:13 says: sing, heavens; rejoice, earth; break out, mountains, "for the Lord has comforted his people". The reason for joy each time is the redemption of a people. On the covenantal reading, the ones who sing are those who are saved. Scripture often uses mountains for rulers and kingdoms (Daniel 2:35), and trees for people (Psalms 1:3; Isaiah 61:3). So the whole picture is of God's people rejoicing. Isaiah 55:12 adds that the trees will clap their hands when God's people go out in joy.
Isaiah 61:3: God's people are called "oaks of righteousness, the planting of the Lord".
Daniel 2:35: the stone becomes a great mountain that fills the whole earth — a kingdom.

Most commentators say Isaiah calls all creation to join in praise, a common poetic form. They do not think mountains and forests are code for people. Some see the singing creation as a hint that redemption will one day reach the whole world.
How do Paul and John use Isaiah 49 (2 Corinthians 6:2; Revelation 7:16-17)?

Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8 as "now is the day of salvation". John uses Isaiah 49:10 for the redeemed multitude. The covenantal reading sees Isaiah's rejoicing heavens and earth fulfilled in the first-century church.

Isaiah 49:8 says God answered his Servant in a time of favour and helped him in a day of salvation, to restore the land. Paul quotes it and says "now is the day of salvation" (2 Corinthians 6:2). (One paper cites Isaiah 49:1 here; the quoted verse is 49:8.) Isaiah 49:10 says the people will not hunger or thirst, nor will the sun strike them, for God will lead them to springs of water. Revelation 7:16-17 applies this to those who come out of the great tribulation. On the covenantal reading, the 144,000 from Israel's tribes are the believing remnant, the first fruits, and the great multitude includes the nations. Isaiah's singing heavens and earth (49:13) are these saved people.
2 Corinthians 6:2 (about AD 56): Paul says Isaiah's day of salvation is "now".
Revelation 14:4 calls the 144,000 "first fruits to God and to the Lamb".

Dispensationalists see the 144,000 as Jewish believers in a future tribulation. Many amillennialists see both the 144,000 and the multitude as the whole church seen two ways. Most accept that Paul sees Isaiah 49 fulfilled in the gospel age.
Why does Isaiah 51:9-11 join creation, the Red Sea and Zion together?
Isaiah tells the exodus as a new creation and promises a second exodus to Zion. The covenantal reading says Hebrews 12 shows that second exodus in the first century.

Isaiah 51:9 calls on the Lord's arm to wake as in days of old. It asks: did you not cut Rahab and pierce the dragon? Rahab is a poetic name for Egypt (Isaiah 30:7; Psalms 87:4). Verse 10 says God dried up the sea and made a road for the redeemed. Verse 11 says the ransomed will return to Zion with singing. Creation words (the deep, the dragon) are used for the exodus. On the covenantal reading, God's acts of creating and redeeming are told in one language. Hebrews 12:18-24 contrasts Mount Sinai with Mount Zion, "the heavenly Jerusalem". Believers had come to Zion. The second exodus was taking place, and a new heaven and earth were being formed.
Psalms 87:4 names "Rahab and Babylon" among the nations: Rahab is Egypt.
Hebrews 12:22: "you have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem."

Most scholars agree Isaiah blends creation and exodus imagery and promises a return from Babylon (538 BC onward). Christian readers widely see a fuller fulfilment in Christ. Traditional readers add that the final fulfilment includes a renewed creation, not only a covenant people.
What does God mean by "that I may plant the heavens and lay the foundations of the earth, and say to Zion, You are my people" (Isaiah 51:16)?
God links the "planting" of heavens and earth with calling Zion his people. The covenantal reading sees this as the clearest text that God's covenant people are his "heaven and earth".

Isaiah 51:15 says, "I am the Lord your God, who divided the sea." Verse 16 says: I have put my words in your mouth and covered you in the shadow of my hand, to plant the heavens, to found the earth, and to say to Zion, "You are my people." The physical heavens were made long before Israel. So this "planting" must be something God did at the exodus and Sinai, when he gave his words and formed a nation. On the covenantal reading, the heavens and earth here are the covenant order and people formed by God's word. The forming of Israel was God's covenant creation. It was his light to the nations.
Isaiah 51:15-16 ties the planting of the heavens to "divided the sea" — the Red Sea at the exodus.
Deuteronomy 4:32-36: Moses compares Sinai with the day God created man on the earth.

Many scholars read verse 16 as God, the Creator of heaven and earth, now acting to restore Zion. The infinitives can mean "I, who planted the heavens". Some see a goal: God plans to "plant" a new heavens and earth in the future (Isaiah 65:17).
What heavens "vanish like smoke" and what earth "wears out like a garment" (Isaiah 51:6)?

Isaiah says the heavens and earth will vanish and wear out, but God's salvation lasts forever. The covenantal reading links this with Hebrews 8:13, where the old covenant is "growing old" and "ready to vanish".

Isaiah 51:4-5 speaks of a law going out from God and his salvation going out to the peoples. Verse 6 says: lift your eyes to the heavens and look at the earth; the heavens will vanish like smoke, and the earth will wear out like a garment, but my salvation will be forever. On the covenantal reading, the New Testament explains this. Hebrews 8:13 says the first covenant is growing old and ready to vanish. Jesus said no one puts new cloth on an old garment (Matthew 9:16). The old covenant was the garment wearing out. The new covenant, God's lasting salvation, replaced it. The time for this was the first century.
